chapters.summary: This chapter contains 20 verses and records Nephi’s introduction to his record and language, and sets the scene in the first year of Zedekiah at Jerusalem. Lehi prays, sees a pillar of fire, and receives a vision of heaven, a descending figure with twelve others, and a book. Reading it, he prophesies Jerusalem’s destruction and Babylonian captivity, and testifies of a coming Messiah. The people mock and seek Lehi’s life.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records the Lord warning Lehi in a dream to flee Jerusalem; Lehi departs with Sariah and sons, leaving property, and travels near the Red Sea to a valley where he builds an altar and names the river Laman. Laman and Lemuel murmur; Lehi rebukes them. Nephi prays, believes, and teaches Sam. The Lord promises prosperity and a land of promise for obedience, and foretells consequences and roles for rebellion.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records Lehi’s dream commanding Nephi and his brothers to return to Jerusalem for Laban’s brass plates containing Jewish records and their genealogy. Nephi agrees; the brothers travel to Jerusalem. Laman’s request is rejected and threatened. They offer their family riches; Laban attempts to kill them and seizes the property. Laman and Lemuel beat Nephi and Sam; an angel commands them to return and promises deliverance.

This chapter contains 38 verses and records Nephi urging his brothers to return to Jerusalem to obtain the brass plates. By night Nephi enters the city, finds Laban drunk, and is constrained by the Spirit to kill him; he beheads Laban and takes his clothing and sword. Disguised, Nephi obtains the plates and brings Laban’s servant Zoram out; Zoram swears to join them. They depart with the plates and Zoram to their father’s camp.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records Lehi’s family rejoicing when Nephi and his brothers return from Jerusalem with the brass plates. Sariah fears her sons have died, complains against Lehi, then is comforted and testifies the Lord protected them. The family offers sacrifices and thanks. Lehi searches the plates, finding the books of Moses, Jewish history to Zedekiah, prophecies including Jeremiah, and his genealogy from Joseph. Lehi prophesies the plates will endure and bless his seed.

This chapter contains 6 verses and records Nephi stating he omits his fathers’ genealogy from these plates because it is in his father’s record, noting they descend from Joseph. He explains space limits and his intent to write about the things of God to persuade people to come to the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He excludes worldly matters and commands his seed to keep the plates focused on what is of worth.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records the Lord commanding Nephi and his brothers to return to Jerusalem to bring Ishmael’s family so the sons can marry. Ishmael’s household joins them, but Laman, Lemuel, and some of Ishmael’s children rebel and want to return. Nephi warns of Jerusalem’s destruction; his brothers bind him, but he prays and is freed. Ishmael’s family pleads; the rebels repent, are forgiven, pray, and all return to Lehi’s tent, offering sacrifices.

This chapter contains 38 verses and records Lehi’s vision in the wilderness: a dark and dreary waste, a man in a white robe, a spacious field, a tree with sweet white fruit, and a river. Lehi beckons Sariah, Nephi, and Sam to partake; Laman and Lemuel refuse. He sees a rod of iron, a strait and narrow path, mist of darkness, and a great and spacious building where people mock. Some hold to the rod and partake; others are lost, drowned, or fall away. Lehi exhorts Laman and Lemuel to keep commandments.

This chapter contains 6 verses and records Nephi explaining that many things Lehi experiences in the valley of Lemuel cannot be written on these plates. Nephi distinguishes between two sets of plates both called the plates of Nephi: one for a fuller history, and these smaller plates commanded by the Lord mainly for the ministry of his people. He notes the other plates cover kings, wars, and contentions, and says the Lord commands this for an unknown wise purpose.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records Lehi prophesying of Jerusalem’s destruction and Babylonian captivity, the Jews’ return, and the coming Messiah about six hundred years after leaving Jerusalem. He mentions prophets testifying, a forerunner who baptizes in Bethabara beyond Jordan, and the Messiah’s death and resurrection with manifestation to Gentiles by the Holy Ghost. It covers Israel scattered and gathered like an olive tree. Nephi desires revelation and warns of judgment and uncleanness.

This chapter contains 36 verses and records Nephi being caught away by the Spirit to a high mountain to see Lehi’s vision. Nephi views the tree of life, then an angel shows Jerusalem and Nazareth, a virgin bearing the Son of God, and identifies the tree and waters as the love of God. Nephi sees Christ’s baptism, ministry, healings, rejection, and crucifixion, and crowds opposing the twelve apostles. The great and spacious building represents worldly pride and falls.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records Nephi’s vision of his seed and his brothers’ seed in the land of promise, including wars, contentions, and many cities. He sees earthquakes, fires, and cities destroyed, then the Lamb of God appears to survivors. Twelve disciples are chosen to minister and judge. Nephi sees generations living righteously, then renewed conflict where his seed is overpowered. The angel explains the river, mists, and great building, and foretells dwindling in unbelief.

This chapter contains 42 verses and records Nephi’s vision of Gentile nations, the rise of a “great and abominable” church, and persecution of saints. It shows Gentiles crossing many waters to the promised land, scattering Nephi’s brethren’s seed, and prospering. A Jewish record goes to Gentiles, is altered by the church, and causes stumbling. The Lamb promises additional plain records from Nephi’s seed to restore truths and unite testimonies to all nations.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records an angel teaching Nephi that Gentiles who repent and hearken to the Lamb are numbered with Israel, while the great and abominable church is destroyed by its own works. Nephi sees two churches, the whore of all the earth, and scattered saints armed with righteousness. Wars and God’s wrath prepare fulfillment of covenants. Nephi sees the apostle John appointed to write remaining visions, which Nephi is forbidden to record.

This chapter contains 36 verses and records Nephi returning from a vision and addressing Laman and Lemuel’s disputing about Lehi’s words. Nephi rebukes their hardness and urges inquiry and commandment keeping, then explains the olive-tree allegory, Gentiles, latter-day covenant, and Israel’s restoration. He interprets Lehi’s dream: the tree of life, iron rod as the word of God, the river as filthiness and an awful gulf/hell, and judgment separating wicked from righteous.

This chapter contains 39 verses and records Nephi exhorting his brothers to keep commandments, their humbling, and marriages to Ishmael’s daughters. The Lord commands Lehi to travel, and the Liahona appears to guide them; they depart, cross the river Laman, camp at Shazer, and hunt. Nephi breaks his steel bow; murmuring follows. Nephi makes a wooden bow; Lehi inquires of the Lord; writings on the ball change with faith. Nephi hunts successfully. Ishmael dies at Nahom; renewed murmuring leads to a plot to kill Lehi and Nephi until the Lord chastens them and they repent.

This chapter contains 55 verses and records Lehi’s family traveling eastward in the wilderness for eight years, arriving at Bountiful by the sea Irreantum. The Lord commands Nephi to build a ship, directs him to ore, and he makes tools and fire. Nephi’s brothers murmur; he recounts Israel’s exodus and warns them. They try to seize him, but God restrains and shocks them; they acknowledge the Lord and are told to worship God and honor parents.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Nephi completing a ship by the Lord’s direction, Lehi’s family loading provisions and sailing, and the births of Jacob and Joseph in the wilderness. Laman and Lemuel bind Nephi; the compass stops and a severe storm threatens the ship until they repent and release him. Nephi prays, the storm ceases, and they reach the promised land, plant seeds, and find animals and ores.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records Nephi making plates of ore by commandment, explaining the division between sacred writings and other records, and directing that the plates be preserved and handed down. It quotes prophets Zenock, Neum, and Zenos about the Messiah’s coming, rejection, crucifixion, burial, and signs, and about Israel’s scattering and future gathering. Nephi teaches his brethren from the brass plates, Moses, and Isaiah, and applies Isaiah to them as a remnant.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records the Lord addressing Jacob/Israel for hypocrisy and obstinacy, declaring foreknowledge of former and new things to prevent credit to idols. He defers anger, refines Israel in affliction, and identifies himself as Creator, the First and the Last. He announces judgment on Babylon and the Chaldeans, calls and prospers his servant, commands departure from Babylon, recalls wilderness water miracles, and states there is no peace to the wicked.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records a prophecy addressing scattered Israel and the isles, describing the Lord’s servant called from the womb to gather Jacob and be a light to the Gentiles. It promises deliverance of prisoners, guidance and provision, and Israel’s gathering from distant lands. Zion laments being forgotten, but the Lord remembers and restores her children through Gentile help, and contends against oppressors.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records Nephi explaining Isaiah’s words to his brothers, saying Israel is scattered among nations and later gathered through Gentile nursing and a mighty Gentile nation on the promised land. He describes the Lord revealing covenants, bringing Israel from captivity, and opposing the great and abominable church. Nephi recounts judgments of fire and conflict, identifies Moses’s prophet as the Holy One of Israel, warns against corrupt churches, and urges repentance, obedience, and enduring.

This chapter contains 32 verses and records Lehi’s final counsel to his sons in the promised land, recounting deliverance from Jerusalem and sea dangers, and his vision of Jerusalem’s destruction. He prophesies the land is for those led by the Lord and is kept from other nations. He promises prosperity for obedience and warns of cursing, invasion, scattering, and bloodshed for unbelief. He urges repentance, unity, and obedience to Nephi, gives conditional blessings to Laman, Lemuel, Sam, and Ishmael’s sons, and blesses Zoram and his descendants.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records Lehi’s counsel to Jacob about afflictions, redemption through the Holy Messiah, and resurrection. It covers law, sin, and atonement; opposition in all things; creation and the Fall of Adam and Eve; the devil’s role; probation and repentance. Lehi teaches human agency to choose liberty and eternal life or captivity and death, and urges obedience to the Mediator’s commandments.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Lehi blessing his son Joseph, promising an inheritance in the land if commandments are kept and that Joseph’s seed will not be destroyed. Lehi recounts covenants made with Joseph in Egypt and quotes Joseph’s prophecy of a latter-day seer like Moses who brings forth God’s word, aided by a spokesman. It covers writings of Joseph and Judah growing together, repentance, and restoration of Israel.

This chapter contains 35 verses and records Lehi blessing the children of Laman and Lemuel, the sons of Ishmael, and Sam, giving commandments about prosperity and being cut off. Lehi dies and is buried. Laman, Lemuel, and Ishmael’s sons become angry with Nephi. Nephi explains his writing purpose, recounts divine help, angels and visions, and offers prayers for deliverance, strength, and trust in God rather than man.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records Nephi’s flight from angry brothers who seek his life, following the Lord’s warning. Nephi leads his family, Zoram, Sam, Jacob, Joseph, sisters, and believers into the wilderness, settles in a place called Nephi, and forms the people of Nephi who keep the law of Moses and prosper. Nephi makes weapons, teaches crafts, builds a temple, consecrates Jacob and Joseph as priests, describes Lamanites being cut off and cursed, and begins new plates amid later wars.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records Jacob addressing the people of Nephi, stating his divine calling and ordination by Nephi, and introducing Isaiah’s words as applicable to the house of Israel. It quotes prophecy about Gentiles and rulers assisting Israel’s children. Jacob reports Jerusalem’s people being slain and taken captive, their future return, the Holy One’s mortal manifestation and crucifixion, subsequent judgments and scattering, and eventual gathering through the Redeemer. It outlines conditions for Gentile salvation, Zion’s enemies, the Messiah’s recovery of Israel, and divine deliverance and vengeance on oppressors.

This chapter contains 11 verses and records the Lord addressing the house of Israel, stating they are not cast off but have sold themselves through iniquity. It affirms God’s power to redeem and deliver, including drying seas and rivers and clothing heavens with blackness. It describes the servant’s obedience, suffering, and confidence in God’s help and vindication. It contrasts those who fear and obey with those who kindle their own light and lie down in sorrow.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records a call to hearken and remember Abraham and Sarah, promises that the Lord comforts Zion and restores her waste places, and declarations of everlasting salvation and righteousness. It urges people not to fear man, recalls the Lord’s past deliverance through the sea, and foretells the redeemed returning to Zion. Jerusalem drinks the cup of fury, then the Lord removes it and gives it to oppressors, commanding Zion and Jerusalem to awake, put on strength, and be loosed from captivity.

This chapter contains 54 verses and records Jacob teaching about the Lord’s covenants with Israel, the fall, death, resurrection, and an infinite atonement. He describes judgment, paradise, hell, and restoration of body and spirit. He commands repentance, faith, baptism, and enduring to the end, explains accountability under law, pronounces woes on specific sins, and urges humility, prayer, and coming to the Holy One of Israel.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Jacob teaching that Christ comes among the Jews and is crucified, followed by judgments, scattering, and later restoration when they believe. It covers Gentile involvement in gathering Israel, promises about a land of inheritance, liberty without kings, and God’s protection of Zion. Jacob urges repentance, freedom to choose life or death, reconciliation to God, and salvation through grace, resurrection, and atonement.

This chapter contains 8 verses and records Nephi’s intent to write Isaiah’s words and apply them to his people and descendants. Nephi states that Isaiah and Jacob have seen the Redeemer, providing multiple witnesses to establish God’s word. He explains that the law of Moses and God’s dealings typify Christ, affirms God’s covenants, and declares that without Christ all perish.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records Isaiah’s prophecy concerning Judah and Jerusalem: in the last days the Lord’s house is established, nations gather to Zion, and the Lord judges so war ceases. It calls the house of Jacob to walk in the Lord’s light, but lists sins of soothsaying, wealth, horses, and idolatry. It warns of the day of the Lord humbling pride, abolishing idols, driving people to hide in rocks, and commands, “Cease ye from man.”

This chapter contains 26 verses and records the Lord removing Jerusalem and Judah’s supports and leaders, resulting in child rulers, oppression, and social disorder. It states Jerusalem and Judah fall because of sins and openly wicked conduct, while the righteous and wicked receive corresponding outcomes. The Lord rises to judge elders and princes for exploiting the poor. It condemns the haughty daughters of Zion and lists removed ornaments, replacing finery with disgrace. Men fall by the sword, and Zion’s gates mourn in desolation.

This chapter contains 6 verses and describes seven women seeking association with one man to remove reproach; the Branch of the Lord and the fruit of the earth benefiting the escaped of Israel; survivors in Zion and Jerusalem being called holy and recorded among the living; the Lord cleansing the daughters of Zion and purging blood from Jerusalem by judgment and burning; and divine protection over Mount Zion with cloud, smoke, fire, and a tabernacle of refuge.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records the song of the Lord’s vineyard, identifying it as Israel and Judah and warning that it is laid waste for producing oppression instead of righteousness. It pronounces woes for greed, drunkenness, ignoring God’s work, drawing iniquity, calling evil good, pride, and corrupt judgment. It foretells captivity, desolation, humiliation, and God summoning distant nations to invade, bringing darkness and sorrow.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records Isaiah’s vision of the Lord on a throne in the temple, with seraphim praising the Lord of Hosts and smoke filling the house. Isaiah laments his unclean lips; a seraph touches his mouth with a coal, purging sin. Isaiah is sent to a people who hear and see but do not understand. Desolation, exile, and a surviving tenth “holy seed” are foretold.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Rezin of Syria and Pekah of Israel attacking Judah under Ahaz, but failing. The Lord sends Isaiah with Shearjashub to counsel Ahaz not to fear and declares the plot to set up Tabeal’s son will not stand. Ahaz refuses to ask a sign; Isaiah gives Immanuel as a sign. Assyria’s coming brings desolation, thorns, and reduced agriculture.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records the Lord commanding Isaiah to write of Maher-shalal-hash-baz and naming his son as a sign that Assyria will take the spoil of Damascus and Samaria. It warns Judah for rejecting Shiloah and predicts Assyria’s overflow into Judah. It instructs not to fear confederacies but to sanctify the Lord. It speaks of stumbling in Israel, sealing the law, rejecting familiar spirits, and resulting distress and darkness.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records prophecy of relief for Zebulun and Naphtali as light comes to those in darkness and oppression is broken. It foretells a child given who reigns on David’s throne with endless government and peace. It then warns Israel, Ephraim, and Samaria of pride, invading enemies (Syrians, Philistines), corrupt leaders, continued divine anger, widespread wickedness, civil strife, and Manasseh and Ephraim opposing Judah.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records woes on unjust rulers who oppress the poor, widows, and fatherless, warning of judgment. The Lord sends Assyria against a hypocritical nation, yet condemns the Assyrian king’s pride and self-exalting boasts. It foretells Assyria’s burning destruction and humbling, and the return of a remnant of Israel to the Lord. It recounts Assyria’s advance through Aiath, Migron, Michmash, Geba, Ramath, Gibeah, Gallim, Laish, Anathoth, Madmenah, Gebim, and Nob toward Zion and Jerusalem.

This chapter contains 16 verses and describes a rod and root of Jesse endowed with the Spirit of the Lord who judges righteously and slays the wicked. It records millennial peace among animals and safety on the Lord’s holy mountain. It covers an ensign sought by Gentiles, the Lord recovering Israel’s remnant from many lands, gathering Judah, ending Ephraim–Judah envy, subduing neighboring nations, drying waters for passage, and a highway from Assyria.

This chapter contains 6 verses and records a hymn of praise to the Lord for turning away anger and giving comfort. It declares God as salvation, strength, and song, and urges trust without fear. It describes drawing water from the wells of salvation with joy. It commands praising, calling on the Lord, declaring his deeds, singing, and shouting in Zion because the Holy One of Israel is present.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records Isaiah’s burden concerning Babylon. It calls nations to assemble for battle under the Lord of Hosts and announces the day of the Lord bringing fear, cosmic darkness, and punishment of the wicked and proud. It foretells Babylon’s overthrow, including the Medes attacking without regard for wealth. Babylon becomes desolate, uninhabited, and filled with wild creatures, while the Lord spares his people.

This chapter contains 32 verses and records the Lord’s future mercy on Jacob and Israel’s restoration to their land, with strangers joining them and former oppressors subdued. It gives a proverb against the king of Babylon, describing his downfall, death, and the cutting off of Babylon’s name and remnant. It mentions Lucifer’s fall, the Lord’s purpose against nations, the Assyrian’s defeat, and an oracle against Palestina after Ahaz’s death, ending with Zion founded as refuge for the poor.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records Nephi explaining Isaiah’s writings and Jewish prophecy, and warning of God’s judgments on nations. Nephi prophesies the Jews’ destruction, Babylonian captivity, return to Jerusalem, later wars, rejection and crucifixion of the Messiah, and Jerusalem’s destruction and scattering. He states the Messiah comes 600 years after Lehi leaves Jerusalem and is Jesus Christ. Nephi teaches salvation through Christ, preservation of the record, grace, and keeping Moses’s law until fulfilled.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records Nephi’s prophecy of Christ’s post-resurrection appearance to his people, signs of the Messiah, and destructions upon the wicked, followed by a period of peace for the righteous and later destruction. It covers last-days coming forth of a sealed book and the role of Gentiles, warnings against pride, false churches, and secret combinations, and commandments against priestcraft, murder, lying, theft, contention, and sexual sin, stating all are invited to salvation.

This chapter contains 35 verses and records prophecies about Gentiles and Jews in the last days, divine judgments, and nations fighting Zion. It describes the coming forth of a sealed book, its delivery to an unlearned man, and the role of three and other witnesses. It notes the learned refuse to read a sealed book, and the Lord commands the sealed portion kept. It covers a “marvelous work,” exposure of secret works, and future restoration where the deaf and blind receive understanding and Jacob’s children sanctify God.

This chapter contains 32 verses and records Nephi’s prophecy of latter-day churches not built unto the Lord that contend, teach by learning, and deny miracles and the Holy Ghost. It describes pride, corruption, persecution of the poor, and false doctrines such as “eat, drink, and be merry.” It warns of the devil’s tactics (anger, carnal security, denying hell) and coming judgment. It pronounces woes on complacency and rejecting more revelation, and calls Gentiles to repent.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records the Lord’s purpose to remember covenants and recover Israel, sending forth additional scripture. It addresses Gentiles who claim the Bible is sufficient, reminding them the Bible comes through the Jews and warning against cursing them. It states God speaks to many nations and commands all peoples to write his words, which will judge the world. It foretells shared records among Jews, Nephites, and lost tribes, and Israel’s gathering.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records Nephi’s warning that all must keep God’s commandments and that repentant Gentiles become the Lord’s covenant people while unrepentant Jews are cast off. It prophesies the book’s coming forth to Gentiles, their carrying it to Nephi’s remnant, and the remnant’s restoration to knowledge of Jesus Christ. It covers scattered Jews believing and gathering, the Lord’s worldwide work, judgment of the wicked, millennial peace, universal revelation, and Satan’s limited power.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records Nephi’s plain statement of the doctrine of Christ. He references the Lamb of God’s baptism, the descent of the Holy Ghost, and the strait and narrow path. He commands repentance, baptism in Christ’s name, receiving the Holy Ghost and baptism of fire, and warns against later denial. He teaches pressing forward, feasting on Christ’s words, and enduring to the end to gain eternal life.

This chapter contains 9 verses and records Nephi teaching what to do after entering “the way”: receive the Holy Ghost, which enables speaking with the tongue of angels and brings the words of Christ. He commands readers to feast on Christ’s words, ask and knock for understanding, and states this is the doctrine of Christ until Christ manifests in the flesh. Nephi urges prayer always, warning against the evil spirit, and instructs praying to the Father in Christ’s name to consecrate actions.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records Nephi’s final testimony and farewell. He says he cannot write all he taught and notes some reject the Holy Spirit and written words. He affirms his prayers for his people and that his writings persuade to do good, teach of the fathers, and speak of Jesus Christ and enduring to the end. He declares charity for Israel, Jews, and Gentiles, urges reconciliation to Christ, and warns that his sealed words will stand at the last judgment.

This chapter contains 19 verses and records Jacob receiving Nephi’s commandment to keep the small plates, writing sacred preachings, revelations, and prophecies about Christ, and passing the record to his seed. It notes Nephi’s old age, appointment of a king, and Nephi’s death. It defines group names as Nephites and Lamanites, reports growing wickedness (many wives, pride, seeking riches), and states Jacob and Joseph are consecrated priests responsible to teach diligently.

This chapter contains 35 verses and records Jacob speaking in the temple after Nephi’s death, declaring God’s word to the Nephites. He condemns pride, costly apparel, and persecution tied to riches, commanding them to seek God first and use wealth to help others. He then condemns whoredoms and plural wives, cites David and Solomon, commands one wife and no concubines, warns of curses, and notes the sorrow of wives and children.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records Jacob exhorting the pure in heart to pray with faith and warning the impure to repent or face a cursed land and Lamanite scourging. He states the Lamanites keep the commandment of one wife and no concubines. He commands the Nephites not to revile the Lamanites, to remember their children, and to awake from sin. He notes further records exist on larger plates and identifies the plates of Jacob.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records Jacob explaining why he writes briefly on plates to preserve a record for his people and descendants. He states that prophets before them know of Christ, keep the law of Moses as pointing to him, and have revelations and prophecy. Jacob urges not to despise revelation, to seek counsel from God, and to be reconciled through Christ’s atonement for resurrection. He describes Jews rejecting prophets and “looking beyond the mark,” and prophesies they will reject the foundational stone, which remains the only sure foundation.

This chapter contains 77 verses and records Zenos’s allegory of the olive tree about the house of Israel. The Lord of the vineyard prunes a tame tree, grafts in wild branches, and plants natural branches in poor and choice ground. After periods of labor, all trees bring corrupt fruit, and the master plans hewing. He spares the vineyard, regrafts natural branches, removes bitter branches gradually, calls additional servants, restores natural fruit, and foretells a final gathering and burning.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records Jacob affirming Zenos’s olive tree prophecy about Israel’s final gathering and the Lord’s servants nourishing the vineyard before the end. He contrasts blessings for diligent laborers with being cast out and the world burned. Jacob urges repentance, not hardening hearts, and accepting prophets’ words about Christ, redemption, and the Holy Ghost, warning of judgment, resurrection, and the lake of fire, and bidding farewell.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records Sherem preaching among the Nephites against Christ and contending with Jacob over the law of Moses and prophecy. Jacob testifies that scriptures and revelations testify of Christ and the atonement. Sherem demands a sign, is smitten and later confesses Christ and deception by the devil before dying. The people are astonished, peace is restored, and they search scriptures. Nephites attempt to reclaim Lamanites, fortify against wars, and Jacob gives the plates to Enos.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records Enos’s prayer in the forest, his receiving forgiveness through faith in Christ, and his intercession for the Nephites and Lamanites. The Lord promises to visit the Nephites by their obedience and covenants to preserve Nephite records to come forth to the Lamanites. Enos preaches and prophesies, notes Nephite agriculture and prophets, describes Lamanite hostility and wars, and closes near death with testimony of Christ.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records Jarom writing briefly by Enos’s command to preserve genealogy and benefit the Lamanites. It notes varying faith among the Nephites, with some receiving revelations. After about 200 years, Nephites keep the law of Moses and Sabbath, grow strong, and fight repeated Lamanite attacks, fortifying cities. It describes prosperity, wealth, tools, and weapons, prophets warning of destruction, and priests and teachers urging repentance and belief in the coming Messiah. Jarom passes the plates to Omni.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records brief writings by Omni, Amaron, Chemish, Abinadom, and Amaleki, including wars with the Lamanites and transfer of the plates through their lineage. It covers Mosiah fleeing the land of Nephi to Zarahemla, uniting with Zarahemla’s people, teaching them his language, and being made king. Mosiah interprets an engraved stone recounting Coriantumr and Jaredite origins. Benjamin succeeds Mosiah, defeats Lamanites, and receives the plates; a failed return to Nephi leaves survivors and missing groups.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records Mormon preparing to deliver his record to Moroni after witnessing Nephite destruction. He explains finding and including additional plates covering prophets from Jacob to King Benjamin and prophecies of Christ. Mormon notes the records’ preservation and judgment. It recounts Benjamin receiving plates, battling Lamanites with the sword of Laban, suppressing false christs and teachers, and restoring peace with prophets amid contention and dissent.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records peace in Zarahemla under King Benjamin, his instruction of sons Mosiah, Helorum, and Helaman in languages, prophecies, and sacred records on the brass plates and plates of Nephi. Benjamin exhorts searching records and keeping commandments to prosper, then prepares to confer the kingdom on Mosiah, commands a gathering proclamation, and entrusts records and sacred items (sword of Laban, director). Mosiah proclaims the gathering to the temple.

This chapter contains 41 verses and records the people gathering at the temple in Zarahemla to hear King Benjamin, offering sacrifices, camping by families, and receiving his words by tower and written copy. Benjamin states he is mortal, recounts his service and labor without taxes, urges mutual service and gratitude to God, and commands obedience. He announces Mosiah as king, warns against contention and the evil spirit, and contrasts outcomes for transgression versus keeping commandments.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records King Benjamin relating an angel’s message about Jesus Christ’s coming: His mortal birth to Mary, miracles, suffering, crucifixion, resurrection, and judgment. It covers the atonement for Adam’s transgression and ignorant sin, and requires repentance and faith for willful rebellion. It notes the law of Moses as types of Christ, declares little children blameless, describes yielding to the Holy Spirit, and warns of judgment and punishment for evil works.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records King Benjamin’s people falling down, pleading for mercy through Christ’s atoning blood, and receiving joy and remission of sins. Benjamin commands belief in God, repentance, humility, prayer, and steadfast faith. He instructs them to live peaceably, teach children, and succor the poor by sharing substance, feeding, clothing, and visiting the sick, in wisdom and order, returning borrowed goods, watching thoughts, words, and deeds, and keeping commandments to avoid perishing.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records King Benjamin asking his people if they believe his words; they affirm faith, report a change of heart through the Spirit, and agree to covenant to obey God. Benjamin declares the covenant acceptable, calls them children of Christ, and commands them to take upon them Christ’s name and retain it without transgression. He contrasts right- and left-hand outcomes and urges steadfast good works.

This chapter contains 7 verses and records King Benjamin taking the names of those who covenant to keep God’s commandments and take upon them the name of Christ, excluding little children. Benjamin consecrates Mosiah as king, gives him charges, and appoints priests to teach and remind the people of their oath before dismissing them home. Mosiah begins reigning at age thirty; Benjamin dies after three years. Mosiah keeps commandments, works the land, and there is no contention for three years.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records Mosiah sending sixteen men led by Ammon from Zarahemla to find Zeniff’s colony in Lehi-Nephi. After wandering, Ammon is seized and brought to King Limhi, who rejoices at news of Zarahemla. Limhi describes Lamanite bondage and heavy tribute, recounts Zeniff’s deception, internal contentions, and the killing of a prophet. He calls the people to repent, trust God, and serve him for deliverance.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records Limhi having Ammon report events since Zeniff and repeat Benjamin’s teachings. Limhi brings the record plates of his people for Ammon to read. Limhi recounts sending 43 men to find Zarahemla; they return with 24 gold plates, breastplates, and rusted swords from a ruined, bone-covered land. Ammon identifies Zarahemla’s king as a seer with interpreters to translate ancient records.

This chapter contains 19 verses and records Zeniff’s account of spying among the Lamanites, opposing his leader’s plan, and returning to Zarahemla after internal fighting. Zeniff leads a second group to the land of Lehi-Nephi, makes a covenant with king Laman for Lehi-Nephi and Shilom, and the people build, repair walls, and farm. After twelve years Laman attacks; Zeniff arms his people, they pray, defeat the Lamanites, and report casualties.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records Zeniff fortifying his people with weapons, guards, farming, and clothmaking, resulting in 22 years of peace. After king Laman dies, his son stirs war; Zeniff uses spies as Lamanites attack near Shilom. Women and children hide; men muster and fight. Zeniff recounts Lamanite traditions about Nephi, hatred, and deception. The Nephites drive out the Lamanites, return to labor, and Zeniff gives the kingdom to a son.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records Noah succeeding Zeniff as king, taking many wives, leading the people into sin, replacing priests, and imposing a one-fifth tax to support himself and his priests. It covers lavish building projects in Shilom and near the temple, Lamanite attacks and a temporary military success, and Abinadi’s prophecy of bondage unless the people repent, prompting attempts to kill him.

This chapter contains 37 verses and records Abinadi returning in disguise to prophesy against King Noah’s people, warning of bondage, afflictions, and Noah’s death unless they repent. The people seize Abinadi and bring him to Noah, who imprisons him and consults the priests. The priests question Abinadi, quoting Isaiah, and he condemns them for perverting the Lord’s ways, neglecting the law of Moses, and seeking riches and immorality. Abinadi cites commandments from Sinai and accuses them of not teaching or keeping them.

This chapter contains 35 verses and records King Noah ordering Abinadi killed, but the people do not seize him as he resists and continues speaking. Abinadi declares he must deliver God’s message, then reads commandments including prohibitions on idolatry, taking God’s name in vain, and breaking the sabbath, and commands honoring parents and avoiding murder, adultery, theft, false witness, and coveting. He rebukes the priests for not teaching these, explains the law of Moses is temporary, and teaches redemption comes through God’s atonement, citing Moses and prophets about the Messiah, resurrection, and suffering.

This chapter contains 12 verses and records Isaiah’s prophecy of the Lord’s servant: he grows up without comeliness, is despised and rejected, bears griefs and sorrows, is wounded for others’ transgressions, and is likened to a lamb led to slaughter without protest. It describes his unjust cutting off, burial with the wicked and rich, being an offering for sin, justifying many, and being rewarded after bearing sins and interceding for transgressors.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records Abinadi teaching that God comes among men as Father and Son, suffers, is crucified, and overcomes death to intercede and redeem. He defines Christ’s “seed” as prophets and believers who heed their words. He quotes Isaiah on publishing peace and salvation. He teaches resurrection, a first resurrection for prophets, the obedient, the ignorant, and little children, and excludes willful rebels. He foresees salvation proclaimed to all nations and Zion/Jerusalem restored.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records Abinadi’s teachings that all peoples will witness the Lord’s salvation and confess God’s just judgments, while the wicked are cast out for refusing to hearken. It covers the Fall, humanity’s lost state, and redemption through Christ’s coming and resurrection. It describes universal resurrection and final judgment by works, with contrasting outcomes, calls to repent, and instructs that the law of Moses is a shadow pointing to redemption through Christ.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records King Noah ordering Abinadi’s death after his teachings. Alma, a young priest and descendant of Nephi, believes Abinadi, pleads for him, is expelled, pursued, escapes, and writes Abinadi’s words. Abinadi is imprisoned, tried, and condemned for saying God will come among men unless he recants. He refuses, warns of judgment, and is burned to death.

This chapter contains 35 verses and records Alma teaching Abinadi’s words privately, including Christ, resurrection, and redemption. Believers gather at the waters of Mormon, covenant to bear burdens, mourn, comfort, and serve God, and Alma baptizes about 204, beginning the church of God. Alma ordains priests and commands repentance, faith, unity, Sabbath observance, weekly worship, self-supporting priests, and giving to the needy. King Noah discovers them, sends an army, and Alma leads about 450 people into the wilderness.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records division among King Noah’s people, Gideon’s attempt to kill Noah, and the approach of a Lamanite army near Shemlon. The people flee; many are killed, and those remaining are spared and taken captive. The Lamanites allow them to possess the land under tribute and surrender of Noah. Noah is burned to death; priests flee. Limhi becomes king, swears tribute, and peace follows for two years under Lamanite guards.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records the priests of Noah kidnapping twenty-four Lamanite daughters at Shemlon. The Lamanites accuse Limhi’s people and march to war; Limhi lays an ambush and a fierce battle follows. The wounded Lamanite king is captured and questioned. Gideon identifies the priests as the culprits. Limhi explains, the king is pacified, meets his army unarmed, and peace is restored.

This chapter contains 36 verses and records Limhi’s people returning to the city of Nephi, then suffering renewed Lamanite oppression and losing three battles. The people humble themselves, cry to God, receive eased burdens, and begin to prosper; Limhi commands support for widows. Limhi seeks Noah’s priests, imprisons Ammon’s party, then rejoices at their Zarahemla origin. A search party finds a destroyed land and ore plates; Ammon mentions Mosiah’s gift to interpret. Limhi and many covenant to serve God and desire baptism, but no authority is present.

This chapter contains 16 verses and records Ammon and King Limhi consulting the people about escape from Lamanite bondage. Gideon proposes using a secret back pass and intoxicating Lamanite guards with tribute wine. Limhi sends wine and gifts; the Lamanites become drunken. Limhi’s people flee by night with families, flocks, provisions, and valuables, travel around Shilom, and reach Zarahemla led by Ammon. Mosiah receives them and their records. Lamanites pursue but lose the trail.

This chapter contains 39 verses and records Alma fleeing king Noah’s armies into the wilderness, settling in Helam, and organizing his people without a king. Alma serves as high priest, consecrates just priests and teachers, and commands love, no contention, and reliance on God. Lamanites invade; Alma’s people surrender and Helam is taken. Noah’s priests under Amulon join the Lamanites; Alma is betrayed, guarded, and Amulon is made ruler under the Lamanite king.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Amulon gaining favor with king Laman and being made a teacher over Lamanite lands, spreading the Nephite language but not teaching God’s law. Amulon persecutes Alma’s people, imposes tasks, and forbids prayer. Alma’s people pray silently; the Lord eases their burdens and promises deliverance. The Lamanites sleep; Alma leads an escape to the valley of Alma, then to Zarahemla after twelve days, where Mosiah receives them.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records King Mosiah gathering the people of Nephi and Zarahemla and reading the records of Zeniff and of Alma’s group. The people react with joy, sorrow, and thanksgiving. Descendants of Amulon reject their fathers’ names and take the name Nephi. Alma preaches repentance and faith, and baptizes Limhi and his people. Mosiah authorizes Alma to establish seven churches with ordained priests and teachers.

This chapter contains 39 verses and records unbelief among the rising generation in Mosiah’s reign, their refusal of baptism, and their deception of church members. Transgressors are brought by teachers and priests to Alma, then to King Mosiah, who gives Alma authority to judge. Alma seeks the Lord and receives instructions on repentance, baptism, forgiveness, and excluding the unrepentant. Alma judges accordingly, removes names of the unrepentant, regulates the church, and the church prospers amid persecution.

This chapter contains 37 verses and records Mosiah’s proclamation stopping persecution of the church and commanding equality, humility, and self-supporting labor by members and priests. It describes Alma the Younger and Mosiah’s sons opposing the church until an angel confronts them; Alma is struck dumb and healed after fasting and prayer. Alma testifies of repentance and new birth, then he and Mosiah’s sons (Ammon, Aaron, Omner, Himni) preach throughout Zarahemla, confessing past sins and strengthening the church amid persecution.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records the sons of Mosiah requesting permission to preach to the Lamanites, Mosiah inquiring of the Lord and granting their mission, and their departure into the wilderness. It covers Mosiah having no heir, translating the Jaredite plates with interpreters (two stones), defining a seer, and the people mourning and learning from the translated account. Mosiah then entrusts the records and interpreters to Alma.

This chapter contains 47 verses and records Mosiah consulting the people about a new king; his sons refuse the throne, so he proposes replacing monarchy with judges chosen by the people. Mosiah warns of contention and the harms of wicked kings, outlines appeals to higher judges, and commands having no king. The people choose judges; Alma becomes first chief judge and high priest. Alma the elder and Mosiah die, ending the reign of kings.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records the first years of the judges, with Alma judging Nehor for priestcraft teachings, the slaying of Gideon, and Nehor’s execution on hill Manti. It covers the spread of priestcraft, laws punishing crime but not belief, persecution and contention involving church members, and disciplinary removals. It describes church equality, labor, and giving to the poor, resulting prosperity, and law-enforced peace through the fifth year.

This chapter contains 38 verses and records Amlici’s campaign to be made king, the vote of the people rejecting him, and his followers consecrating him anyway. The Amlicites and Nephites arm and battle at hill Amnihu near the river Sidon, with heavy casualties. Alma camps in the valley of Gideon, sends spies, learns the Amlicites join Lamanites in Minon, and fights them at Sidon, slaying Amlici. The enemies flee toward the wilderness Hermounts.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records Nephites burying the dead and returning home after heavy losses near the river Sidon. It describes Amlicites marking their foreheads red like Lamanites, and Lamanite appearance and identifying marks. It recounts the curse and mark placed on Laman and Lemuel’s descendants, separation from Nephites, and consequences of mixing or fighting against Nephi’s seed. Another Lamanite army attacks; Alma, wounded, sends an army that drives them out, ending fifth-year wars.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records events in the sixth through ninth years of the judges: peace in Zarahemla, mourning and losses from Lamanite destruction, and renewed church growth with baptisms in Sidon led by Alma. It covers rising pride and persecution among church members, resulting contentions and inequality. Alma appoints Nephihah as chief judge and relinquishes the judgment-seat to preach and retain the high priesthood.

This chapter contains 62 verses and records Alma preaching in Zarahemla, recounting his father’s church in Mormon and deliverance from Noah’s people and the Lamanites. He questions the church about remembering captivity, experiencing a change of heart, and being judged by works. He commands repentance, humility, avoiding pride and persecution, caring for the poor, and producing good fruit. Alma testifies by the Spirit of Jesus Christ’s coming and invites all to be baptized.

This chapter contains 8 verses and records Alma ordaining priests and elders in Zarahemla by laying on hands to preside over the church. Repentant nonmembers are baptized and received, while unrepentant members are rejected and their names blotted out. The church order is established, the word is available to all, and believers are commanded to gather often for fasting and prayer. Alma then travels east of Sidon to the valley and city of Gideon and teaches the church there.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records Alma speaking at Gideon after leaving the judgment-seat, expressing hope the people are faithful, and urging repentance and preparation for the Son of God. He prophesies Christ’s birth to Mary at Jerusalem and describes his suffering, death, and taking sins and infirmities. Alma commands being born again, baptism, covenant keeping, humility, patience, prayer, gratitude, and having faith, hope, and charity, then pronounces blessings and peace.

This chapter contains 32 verses and records Alma returning from Gideon to Zarahemla, then preaching and baptizing in Melek. He travels to Ammonihah, is rejected, reviled, and cast out. An angel commands Alma to return and warn of destruction unless the people repent. Alma meets Amulek, is fed, stays with him, then both are called to preach repentance, filled with the Holy Ghost, and given power amid imprisonment.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records Alma, commanded by God, preaching again in Ammonihah with Amulek. The people contend, question his authority, and attempt to seize him. Alma recounts Lehi’s deliverance, warns that prosperity depends on keeping commandments, and calls them to repent or face destruction, including invasion by Lamanites. He cites angelic warnings and prophesies the Son of God’s coming to redeem the repentant. The Lord prevents Alma’s imprisonment; Amulek begins preaching.

This chapter contains 32 verses and records Amulek preaching in Ammonihah, giving his lineage and reporting an angel’s command to receive and feed Alma. He bears witness of Alma’s message and blessings on his household. Lawyers question Amulek to trap him, but he perceives their intent, warns of destruction if the people reject the righteous, and cites Mosiah’s warning about choosing iniquity. The people accuse him; Zeezrom is introduced as chief accuser.

This chapter contains 46 verses and records Mosiah’s law on judges’ wages and debt enforcement, lists Nephite gold and silver measures and values, and notes lawyers stir up contention for gain against Alma and Amulek. Zeezrom questions and offers Amulek money to deny God. Amulek testifies of one God, the Son of God’s coming, repentance, resurrection, and final judgment; Zeezrom trembles.

This chapter contains 37 verses and records Alma addressing Zeezrom and the people, exposing his deceit and warning of the devil’s snares. Alma explains that mysteries are given according to heed and a softened heart; hardened hearts receive less and are led to destruction. He teaches resurrection and judgment by works, including a second spiritual death for the unrepentant. Answering Antionah, Alma recounts Adam’s fall, the tree of life restriction, probationary life, angels, commandments, redemption, repentance, and entering God’s rest.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records Alma teaching about priests and high priests ordained after the holy order of the Son, called from the foundation of the world to teach commandments and lead people to enter God’s rest. He describes sanctification through faith, repentance, and the Holy Ghost. He cites Melchizedek, king of Salem, and Abraham paying tithes. Alma warns against wresting scriptures, urges immediate repentance, and commands humility, prayer, watchfulness, and enduring faith, hope, and love.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records many in Ammonihah believing Alma and Amulek, while others bind them and accuse them before the chief judge. Zeezrom confesses guilt and is cast out. Believers, their wives and children, and scriptures are burned, and Alma and Amulek are imprisoned, beaten, mocked, and deprived. On the twelfth day Alma prays; they break their cords, an earthquake destroys the prison and kills their persecutors, and they escape as the people flee.

This chapter contains 19 verses and records Alma and Amulek fleeing Ammonihah to Sidom, where they meet believers who were cast out. Zeezrom lies sick with a fever and guilt, sends for them, affirms belief in Christ, and is healed through Alma’s prayer, then baptized and begins preaching. Alma establishes a church in Sidom and ordains priests and teachers as many are baptized. Ammonihah remains unrepentant. Amulek loses wealth and family support; Alma and Amulek return to Zarahemla.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records Lamanite armies destroying Ammonihah, taking captives, and Zoram with sons Lehi and Aha seeking Alma’s guidance. Alma prophesies the Lamanite route; the Nephite army meets them east of Sidon near Manti, rescues all captives, and drives the Lamanites away. Ammonihah becomes the Desolation of Nehors. After years of peace, Alma, Amulek, and others preach repentance, condemn sins, and teach Christ’s coming, death, resurrection, and appearance after resurrection.

This chapter contains 39 verses and records Alma meeting the sons of Mosiah as they return after fourteen years preaching among the Lamanites, marked by scripture study, prayer, fasting, and hardships. It recounts their departure from Zarahemla, refusal of kingship, and separation to preach. Ammon goes to Ishmael, is taken before King Lamoni, becomes his servant, and defends the king’s flocks at Sebus by slinging stones, cutting off attackers’ arms, and returning the flocks, bringing the severed arms as evidence to the king.

This chapter contains 43 verses and records King Lamoni hearing his servants testify of Ammon defending the flocks at Sebus. Lamoni assumes Ammon is the Great Spirit, then questions him; Ammon discerns Lamoni’s thoughts and says he is a man empowered by God. Ammon teaches about God, creation, Adam, the fall, Lehi’s departure from Jerusalem, wilderness journey, rebellions, the plan of redemption, and Christ. Lamoni prays, falls as if dead, and lies two days while his family mourns.

This chapter contains 36 verses and records Ammon visiting Lamoni’s queen, declaring Lamoni is not dead, and Lamoni rising the next day. Lamoni testifies he has seen the Redeemer; the king, queen, Ammon, and servants fall prostrate by the Spirit. Abish gathers the people; a man trying to kill Ammon falls dead. Abish raises the queen and king, who teach the crowd. Many believe, are baptized, and a church is established among the Lamanites.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records Ammon receiving revelation to go with King Lamoni to Middoni to free Aaron, Muloki, and Ammah from prison. On the journey they meet Lamoni’s father, king over all the land, who orders Lamoni to kill Ammon and return to Ishmael. Ammon resists, disables the king’s arm, and secures the prisoners’ release and Lamoni’s independence. They reach Middoni and free the brethren, who recount their afflictions and imprisonment.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records Aaron traveling to the Lamanite city Jerusalem near Mormon, preaching in Nehorite synagogues, and disputing with Amalekites who reject repentance, angels, and Christ. Aaron teaches from scriptures about Christ, resurrection, and redemption. He joins Muloki at Ani-Anti, then goes to Middoni where some are imprisoned and later freed by Lamoni and Ammon. They preach widely; Lamoni builds synagogues in Ishmael, grants worship liberty, and Ammon teaches his people.

This chapter contains 35 verses and records Aaron and his brethren visiting the Lamanite king over the land of Nephi. Aaron teaches the king about God, creation, the fall, Christ’s redemption, and faith and repentance; the king prays, falls as if dead, and is raised by Aaron, leading to the conversion of his household and permission to preach. It also outlines Lamanite and Nephite geography, borders, seas, the narrow neck, and lands Bountiful and Desolation.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records the Lamanite king’s proclamation protecting Ammon, Aaron, Omner, Himni, and other preachers from harm, imprisonment, or expulsion, granting access to homes and places of worship. Aaron and the missionaries travel city to city, establish churches, and ordain priests and teachers. Thousands convert in Ishmael, Middoni, Nephi, Shilom, Shemlon, Lemuel, and Shimnilom, lay down weapons, and do not fall away. Amalekites and Amulonites largely reject. Converts take the name Anti-Nephi-Lehies and correspond with Nephites.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records Amalekites and Amulonites stirring unconverted Lamanites to war against the people of Anti-Nephi-Lehi. The king gives the kingdom to his son Anti-Nephi-Lehi and dies. Ammon and brethren counsel with Lamoni and Anti-Nephi-Lehi; the converts refuse weapons, bury them, and covenant not to shed blood. Invaders kill 1,005; many attackers repent, drop weapons, and join them, mostly Lamanite descendants.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records Lamanite retaliation after slaying their brethren, including attacks on Ammonihah and battles with the Nephites. It reports the destruction of much of Amulon’s seed, their persecution of believing Lamanites by fire, and Lamanites then hunting Amulon’s remnant, fulfilling Abinadi’s words. Many Lamanites join Anti-Nephi-Lehi, bury weapons, keep commandments and the law of Moses while looking to Christ. Ammon and Aaron’s group rejoices.

This chapter contains 37 verses and records Ammon rejoicing with his brethren over success preaching to the Lamanites after leaving Zarahemla. He credits God for bringing thousands into the fold and for deliverance amid afflictions, imprisonment, and persecution. Aaron cautions against boasting; Ammon states he boasts in God’s power and mercy. Ammon recounts their former opposition to the church, the Lord’s command to be patient, and notes converts bury weapons and refuse to kill.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records Amalekites stirring Lamanites to attack the Anti-Nephi-Lehies, who refuse to take up arms and are slain. Ammon consults the Lord and is commanded to lead them from the land of Nephi toward Zarahemla. Ammon meets Alma, reports to the chief judge, and the people grant the land of Jershon with Nephite protection. The converts settle in Jershon as the people of Ammon and remain unwilling to shed blood.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records a major battle after the people of Ammon and a church are established in Jershon and Nephite armies surround Zarahemla. Many Lamanites and Nephites are slain; the Lamanites are driven and scattered. The land mourns with fasting and prayer, ending the fifteenth year of the judges. It summarizes Ammon’s missions, wars, widespread death, differing hopes for the dead, sin’s effects, and a call to diligence.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records Alma’s desire to preach repentance to all people, then his acknowledgment that he must be content with his calling. It covers God granting according to human desires and accountability for choosing good or evil. Alma rejoices in bringing souls to repentance, recalls deliverance from bondage and the establishment of the church, praises his brethren’s success in the land of Nephi, and prays for their salvation.

This chapter contains 60 verses and records peace in the 16th–17th years of the judges, Nephite observance of the law of Moses, and the rise of Korihor in Zarahemla preaching against prophecy, Christ, and accountability. Korihor is expelled from Jershon, taken in Gideon, and brought to Alma. After disputation and demanding a sign, Korihor is struck dumb, confesses deception, is cast out begging, and is killed among the Zoramites.

This chapter contains 38 verses and records Alma hearing that the Zoramites in Antionum pervert God’s ways and may align with the Lamanites. Alma leads Ammon, Aaron, Omner, Amulek, Zeezrom, and sons Shiblon and Corianton to preach. They observe Zoramite weekly worship using the Rameumptom and a set prayer denying Christ and claiming election. Alma prays for strength and success, blesses his companions, and they receive the Holy Spirit and divine provision.

This chapter contains 43 verses and records Alma preaching to the poor cast out of synagogues on the hill Onidah. Alma teaches that worship is not limited to synagogues and explains humility, repentance, mercy, and enduring to the end. He defines faith as hope in unseen true things and urges belief without demanding signs. He compares the word to a seed to be planted, tested, and nourished until it grows into a tree bearing fruit unto everlasting life.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records Alma answering the Zoramites’ questions about faith and worship after being cast out of synagogues. He says they can worship God anywhere and urges them to search the scriptures. Alma quotes Zenos on prayer in wilderness, field, house, closet, and congregations, and on mercy through God’s Son. He cites Zenock and Moses’s serpent type, warns against hard-hearted unbelief, teaches redemption, Atonement, resurrection, judgment, and commands them to plant and nourish the word by faith.

This chapter contains 41 verses and records Amulek teaching the Zoramites about Christ’s coming and the need for an infinite, eternal atonement that fulfills the law of Moses. He explains mercy and justice, urges faith unto repentance, continual prayer in all places, and charity to the needy. He warns against procrastinating repentance, describes the state after death, and exhorts humility, taking Christ’s name, resisting the devil, patience in afflictions, and hope of rest.

This chapter contains 16 verses and records Alma, Amulek, and their brethren withdrawing to Jershon after preaching to the Zoramites. Zoramite leaders reject the message, secretly gauge public opinion, and cast out many believers, who are received and supported by the people of Ammon in Jershon. Zoramites threaten Ammon, ally with the Lamanites, and prepare for war; Ammon moves to Melek and Nephite armies occupy Jershon. Alma returns to Zarahemla, grieves over wickedness and conflict, and gathers his sons to give individual charges.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records Alma counseling his son Helaman to keep God’s commandments and remember past deliverances from captivity. Alma recounts his attempt with the sons of Mosiah to destroy the church, the angel’s appearance, and his three-day torment over sin. He cries to Jesus Christ for mercy, receives relief, joy, and strength, and then labors to bring others to repentance. He testifies of God’s deliverance and final judgment.

This chapter contains 47 verses and records Alma commanding Helaman to keep the Nephite records, brass plates, and sacred items, promising preservation for God’s purposes and warning that transgression brings loss. Alma addresses the twenty-four plates and interpreters used to reveal past secret works while withholding their oaths and signs. He instructs Helaman to teach repentance, faith in Christ, humility, diligence, and to seek God’s guidance. He describes the Liahona’s operation by faith and uses it to compare heeding the word of Christ to reaching a promised land.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records Alma’s counsel to his son Shiblon: keep God’s commandments to prosper, trust God for deliverance, and endure faithfully. Alma recalls Shiblon’s patience among the Zoramites and his own conversion by an angel and mercy through Jesus Christ. He commands diligence and temperance, warns against pride and idle boasting, urges boldness without overbearance, bridling passions, humble prayer, and teaching the word.

This chapter contains 19 verses and records Alma’s counsel to his son Corianton, contrasting him with his steady brother and rebuking Corianton’s boasting and misconduct with Isabel in Siron, where he forsakes the ministry. Alma calls sexual sin an abomination, warns of unforgivable denial of the Holy Ghost and difficulty of forgiveness for murder, and commands repentance, self-denial, and seeking counsel from older brothers. He urges acknowledging faults to the Zoramites, avoiding riches, and proclaiming Christ’s coming and redemption.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records Alma teaching his son Corianton about the resurrection. He states resurrection occurs after Christ and that a time is appointed, with a space between death and resurrection. Spirits return to God; the righteous enter paradise and rest, and the wicked enter darkness and misery. Alma distinguishes spirit states from bodily resurrection, describes restoration of body and soul, and judgment according to works.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records Alma explaining to his son the doctrine of restoration: resurrection restores soul to body and all things to proper order. People are judged by works and heart’s desires, receiving good for good or evil for evil, happiness or misery. God’s decrees are unalterable; individuals choose. Alma warns restoration does not return sin to happiness, defines restoration as like for like, and commands mercy, justice, righteous judgment, and continual good.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records Alma explaining to his son the justice of God in punishing sin. He recounts Adam and Eve being cast from Eden, barred from the tree of life, and given a probationary time to repent. He outlines temporal and spiritual death, law and punishment, and repentance. He states mercy operates through an atonement, bringing resurrection, restoration to God’s presence, and judgment by works, urging repentance and preaching.

This chapter contains 54 verses and records the start of war in the eighteenth year of the judges as Zoramites join the Lamanites under Zerahemnah. Moroni, age twenty-five, leads the Nephite armies, equips them with armor, and gathers forces at Jershon. The Lamanites march toward Manti by the Sidon; Alma inquires and warns Moroni. Moroni uses spies and stratagem, with Lehi’s force, to encircle the Lamanites near hill Riplah and the river Sidon, driving them to terror; Moroni commands his men to stop shedding blood.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records Moroni confronting Zerahemnah after the Lamanites are surrounded, commanding them to surrender weapons and covenant not to return to war. Zerahemnah refuses to swear, attacks, and is scalped by a Nephite soldier. Many Lamanites surrender and make a peace covenant; others fight until Zerahemnah agrees. The dead are cast into the waters of Sidon, and Nephite armies return home, ending the eighteenth year.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records Nephite rejoicing, fasting, and prayer after deliverance. Alma questions Helaman about the records, belief in Jesus Christ, and keeping commandments, then gives a sealed prophecy of Nephite decline and extinction about four hundred years after Christ’s manifestation. Alma blesses Helaman, his other sons, the land, and the church, then departs from Zarahemla and is no more heard of. Helaman and brethren reestablish the church, appoint priests and teachers, and face dissension and pride from riches.

This chapter contains 41 verses and records Amalickiah stirring dissension among Nephites and seeking kingship, causing some church members to dissent. Moroni raises the title of liberty, calls the people to covenant to defend God, religion, freedom, families, and maintain commandments. Moroni pursues Amalickiah toward the land of Nephi, captures remaining Amalickiahites, and executes covenant refusers. Standards are raised on towers; peace returns. Helaman and high priests keep church order; deaths occur by faith, fevers, and old age.

This chapter contains 36 verses and records Amalickiah stirring the Lamanites to war and receiving command to compel dissenters. He schemes at Onidah and mount Antipas, negotiates with Lehonti, and has Lehonti poisoned to become chief commander. Amalickiah returns to the city of Nephi, arranges the king’s assassination, and frames the king’s servants, who flee to Zarahemla and join the people of Ammon. He takes the city, convinces the queen, marries her, and is acknowledged king over Lamanites and Nephite dissenters.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Amalickiah stirring the Lamanites to anger, appointing Zoramite chief captains, and marching toward Zarahemla to bring Nephites into bondage. It describes Moroni fortifying Nephite cities with forts, earthworks, and stone walls, and teaching defensive warfare to preserve liberty, families, and religion. It notes Helaman and others preaching and baptizing, four years of internal peace, then renewed wars with reluctant Nephite resistance.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records Lamanite armies approaching rebuilt Ammonihah and being thwarted by Moroni’s fortifications. The Lamanites retreat to attack the city of Noah, where Lehi commands and defenses include banks, ditches, and guarded entrances. Lamanite assaults fail; chief captains are slain and over a thousand die, while no Nephites are killed and about fifty are wounded. Amalickiah reacts with anger and oaths, while Nephites give thanks; the year ends with peace and church prosperity under Helaman, Shiblon, Corianton, and Ammon.

This chapter contains 40 verses and records Moroni fortifying Nephite cities with earthworks, timbers, pickets, and towers, driving Lamanites from the east wilderness, and securing borders from sea to sea near Sidon and Bountiful. Nephites found cities Moroni, Nephihah, and Lehi and prosper through years of peace. A land dispute leads Morianton to attempt flight north; Teancum stops them near Desolation, kills Morianton, and returns prisoners. Nephihah dies, and Pahoran becomes chief judge.

This chapter contains 37 verses and records political contention in the 25th year as king-men seek to alter the law and replace Chief Judge Pahoran, but the freemen prevail by popular vote. Moroni receives authority to compel the king-men to defend the country; 4,000 are slain and others imprisoned or compelled to support liberty. Meanwhile Amalickiah invades, captures Moroni and several eastern seashore cities, is checked near Bountiful by Teancum, and is killed by Teancum at night.

This chapter contains 40 verses and records Teancum’s response to Amalickiah’s death, the Lamanite retreat to Mulek, and Ammoron becoming king. Moroni orders prisoner retention for ransom and fortifies Bountiful and the narrow pass. Ammoron attacks by the west sea while others harass the east. Moroni and Teancum decoy Jacob’s forces from Mulek; Moroni retakes the city, Lehi helps surround the Lamanites, Jacob is killed, Moroni is wounded, many surrender, and numerous prisoners are taken.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records Moroni and Lehi securing Mulek, guarding Lamanite prisoners, and using them to bury the dead and fortify Bountiful with ditches and earthworks. It notes Nephite dissensions that allow Lamanites to take western cities. It recounts the people of Ammon’s oath against bloodshed, Helaman preventing them from breaking it, and 2,000 of their sons covenanting to fight under Helaman, who marches to the southwest borders.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records correspondence about exchanging prisoners in the twenty-ninth year of the judges. Ammoron proposes an exchange; Moroni seeks Nephite captives, cites Lamanite capture of women and children, and demands one man, wife, and children per prisoner, threatening retaliation. Ammoron replies in anger, claims Nephites murdered Amalickiah, asserts Lamanite right to rule, agrees to exchange for provisions, denies knowledge of God, and identifies as a Zoramite descendant.

This chapter contains 35 verses and records Moroni refusing a prisoner exchange with Ammoron, then using a Lamanite-descended man named Laman to deceive guards at the city of Gid with strong wine. While the guards sleep drunken, Moroni arms Nephite prisoners, surrounds the Lamanites, and gains the city without slaughter. He frees prisoners, takes Lamanites captive for fortification work, resists poisoning attempts, and prepares to attack fortified Morianton as the 29th year ends.

This chapter contains 57 verses and records Helaman’s epistle to Moroni about the war in the south. Helaman leads 2,000 sons of the people Ammon brought from the land of Nephi to aid Antipus at Judea as Lamanites hold Manti, Zeezrom, Cumeni, and Antiparah. Reinforcements and provisions arrive from Zarahemla and the stripling soldiers’ fathers. Helaman and Antipus use a feigned supply march to draw Antiparah’s army, fight, Antipus is killed, Lamanites are surrounded, captured, and sent to Zarahemla; none of the 2,000 die.

This chapter contains 36 verses and records Helaman refusing Ammoron’s offer to trade Antiparah for prisoners, after which Antiparah is abandoned and taken. In the twenty-ninth year Helaman receives reinforcements, surrounds Cumeni, intercepts Lamanite provisions, and compels the city’s surrender. Prisoners revolt and many are slain; others escape. Ammoron sends an army, but the 2,060 sons of the Ammonites help defeat it, preserving Cumeni with heavy losses.

This chapter contains 41 verses and records Helaman’s report to Moroni about the campaign to regain Manti. He waits for reinforcements from Zarahemla, receives limited provisions and 2,000 men, and prays for deliverance. Helaman uses a wilderness stratagem with Gid and Teomner to draw out the Lamanites, seize Manti without bloodshed, and cause enemy retreat. He notes captured women and children, small Nephite forces, questions government support, and reports the sons of Ammon survive though wounded and keep commandments.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records Moroni rejoicing over Helaman’s success and informing nearby people. Moroni sends an epistle to Pahoran in Zarahemla requesting reinforcements for Helaman and plans to recover remaining cities. Lamanites, strengthened by refugees under Ammoron, attack Nephihah and cause great slaughter; survivors flee to Moroni’s army. Nephihah is lost; Moroni and captains sorrow and doubt because of wickedness, and Moroni is angry at governmental indifference.

This chapter contains 36 verses and records Moroni’s epistle to Pahoran in Zarahemla, condemning the government’s neglect to send men and provisions to his and Helaman’s armies. Moroni describes suffering, heavy losses, and Lamanite occupation and captives, blaming internal dissension and king-men. He calls leaders to repent, remember deliverances, and act, warning of judgment and threatening to come raise insurrections or use the sword unless aid is sent.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records Pahoran’s reply to Moroni, explaining a rebellion that drives him from Zarahemla to Gideon and withholds provisions. Pahoran reports dissenters seize Zarahemla, appoint a king, and ally with the Lamanites. He affirms defending liberty, resists rebellion, and trusts God for deliverance. He asks Moroni to come with men, support Lehi and Teancum, gather forces, retake Zarahemla, and send provisions.

This chapter contains 52 verses and records Moroni uniting with Pahoran in Gideon, defeating Pachus, restoring Pahoran to the judgment-seat, and executing dissenters who refuse to defend freedom. Moroni sends reinforcements to Helaman, Lehi, and Teancum, then retakes Nephihah by night stratagem; Lamanite prisoners covenant and join the people of Ammon. Teancum kills Ammoron and is slain; Moroni drives out the Lamanites, fortifies lands, yields command to Moronihah, and peace and church regulations are reestablished; Helaman later dies.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records Shiblon taking custody of the sacred records, and the deaths of Moroni and later Shiblon. It covers Hagoth building ships near Bountiful by Desolation, with thousands migrating northward; one ship returns, others are lost at sea, and Corianton sails north with provisions. Shiblon transfers the records to Helaman’s son Helaman. Dissenters join the Lamanites, who attack Moronihah but are defeated.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records contention after Pahoran dies, as his sons Pahoran, Paanchi, and Pacumeni vie for the judgment-seat. Pahoran is chosen, Paanchi is tried and executed, and Kishkumen murders Pahoran and forms a secret covenant. Pacumeni becomes chief judge. In the forty-first year, Lamanites under Coriantumr seize Zarahemla and kill Pacumeni; Moronihah and Lehi defeat them, slay Coriantumr, retake Zarahemla, and release prisoners.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records Helaman’s appointment to the judgment-seat in the forty-second year of the judges. Kishkumen, who murdered Pahoran, plots to kill Helaman with a secret band led by Gadianton. A servant learns their plan by disguise, meets Kishkumen, and kills him. Helaman orders the band captured, but Gadianton leads them into the wilderness by a secret route.

This chapter contains 37 verses and records contention and dissensions in years 43–48, including migrations from Zarahemla to the land northward, settlement near large waters, cement building, shipping timber, and growth of cities and temples. It notes extensive Nephite recordkeeping and later Nephite decline. Helaman judges with justice, names sons Nephi and Lehi, and peace returns while Gadianton’s secret combinations persist. Many join the church by baptism; later pride brings persecution. Helaman dies; Nephi succeeds.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records dissensions and bloodshed among Nephites, dissenters joining Lamanites, and a Lamanite campaign that captures Zarahemla and most lands southward, driving Moronihah into Bountiful to fortify. Moronihah later regains many cities and about half the lands. It lists Nephite sins, describes preaching by Moronihah, Nephi, and Lehi, notes repentance and partial recovery, then continued stalemate, fear, corrupt laws, dwindling church, and loss of divine preservation.

This chapter contains 52 verses and records Nephi giving the judgment-seat to Cezoram and choosing to preach with Lehi amid corrupt government. Helaman’s counsel to his sons is quoted, urging commandments, remembrance, and faith in Christ and repentance. Nephi and Lehi preach through Nephite cities and among Lamanites, baptizing many. They are imprisoned, surrounded by fire, and a voice commands repentance; darkness disperses, angels minister, about three hundred witness, and many Lamanites lay down weapons and yield lands.

This chapter contains 41 verses and records increased Lamanite righteousness and Nephite wickedness, with Lamanites preaching in Zarahemla and Nephi and Lehi preaching northward. It covers peace, free travel and trade, wealth, and the naming of lands Lehi (south) and Mulek (north). Cezoram and his son are murdered; Gadianton and Kishkumen’s secret band grows among Nephites, while Lamanites destroy it among themselves. The robbers gain control of Nephite government by the 68th year.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records Nephi son of Helaman returning to Zarahemla after preaching in the land northward and being rejected. He laments widespread wickedness, with Gadianton robbers controlling judgment-seats and corruption in government. From a tower in his garden by the highway to the market, he addresses gathered people, commands repentance, warns of scattering, loss of cities and lands, and destruction, and declares the Lord reveals these warnings.

This chapter contains 28 verses and records judges in the secret band of Gadianton accusing Nephi and stirring the people against him, though they fear to seize him. Nephi cites Moses and prophets as witnesses of the coming Messiah and Jerusalem’s destruction, including Mulek and Lehi’s flight.
