He rebukes the people for rejecting evidence and warns of imminent judgment, declaring their chief judge is murdered by his brother, both Gadianton members.

This chapter contains 41 verses and records five men verifying Nephi’s prophecy by finding Chief Judge Seezoram dead. The people wrongly accuse and imprison the five, then suspect Nephi of conspiracy. Nephi is questioned at the burial and gives a sign naming Seantum, Seezoram’s brother, as the murderer. Seantum is confronted, found with blood, confesses, and Nephi and the five are freed. Some believe Nephi is a prophet; others call him a god.

This chapter contains 19 verses and records Nephi left alone after the people divide, then hears the Lord commend his preaching and grant power to seal and loose, and to smite the earth with famine, pestilence, and destruction according to wickedness. The Lord commands Nephi to warn the people to repent or be destroyed. Nephi returns preaching; many harden their hearts, revile him, and try to imprison him, but the Spirit conveys him away. He preaches from multitude to multitude as contentions and slayings increase, ending the 71st year.

This chapter contains 38 verses and records wars among the Nephites caused by a secret band of robbers in the 72nd–73rd years. Nephi prays for famine; drought and famine strike Nephites and Lamanites, causing widespread death. The people repent, sackcloth, and the Gadianton band becomes extinct. Nephi prays again; rain returns in the 76th year, bringing peace and church growth through the 78th. Later dissenters form new Gadianton robbers; wars and failed expeditions follow, leading to renewed pride and iniquity through the 85th year.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records Mormon’s reflections on human unsteadiness: people prosper, forget God, and require chastening by afflictions, death, famine, and pestilence. It states God’s power to command earth, mountains, waters, and the length of day, and to curse hidden treasures and individuals for iniquity. It declares repentance as the means of salvation and contrasts final outcomes of everlasting life versus damnation.

This chapter contains 39 verses and records Samuel the Lamanite preaching repentance at Zarahemla from the city wall after being cast out. He prophesies destruction within 400 years unless the Nephites repent and have faith in Jesus Christ. He warns Zarahemla, Gideon, and surrounding cities, foretells curses on the land and “slippery” hidden treasures, condemns persecuting prophets and trusting flattering teachers, and declares probation ending through procrastination.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records Samuel the Lamanite prophesying signs of the Son of God’s birth in five years, including a night without darkness and a new star, and calling the people to repent. He also prophesies signs of Christ’s death: three days of darkness, thunderings, earthquakes, broken rocks, tempests, desolated cities, and opened graves with saints appearing. He teaches resurrection, repentance versus condemnation, and human agency to choose good or evil.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records Samuel warning the Nephites to repent or face desolation, mourning, and destruction despite signs and wonders. He contrasts them with many Lamanites who keep the law of Moses, seek to convert others, believe scripture, repent, and bury weapons. He states the Lord prolongs and will later restore the Lamanites though they are scattered, but will utterly destroy unrepentant Nephites.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records reactions to Samuel the Lamanite’s prophecy: believers seek Nephi, confess sins, and are baptized; unbelievers attack Samuel with stones and arrows but cannot hit him, then try to seize him, and he escapes to preach in his own country. It summarizes years 86–90 of the judges, noting continued pride, increasing wickedness, signs and angels appearing, and widespread skepticism, contention, and rumors stirred up by Satan.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records the transfer of sacred records to Nephi’s son as Lachoneus governs. Unbelievers set a day to kill believers unless Samuel’s sign occurs; Nephi prays and the Lord promises the sign and Christ’s birth. Night has no darkness and a new star appears. Many repent and are baptized; debate over the law of Moses ends. Later years are mostly peaceful but Gadianton robbers grow through Nephite dissenters and Zoramite influence among Lamanite youth.

This chapter contains 19 verses and records the people forgetting earlier signs, hardening their hearts, and growing in wickedness as years 95–100 pass, with time reckoned from the sign of Christ’s coming. Nephi, keeper of the records, does not return to Zarahemla and cannot be found. In the thirteenth year wars intensify with numerous Gadianton robbers; converted Lamanites unite with Nephites, are numbered as Nephites, and fight for safety and worship. Fighting continues through years 14–15 with shifting advantages and increasing afflictions.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records Giddianhi’s epistle to governor Lachoneus demanding Nephite lands and submission, with threats of destruction by Gadianton robbers. Lachoneus rejects it, calls the people to pray and repent, proclaims a gathering of families and supplies, and orders strong fortifications and guards. Gidgiddoni is appointed chief commander, forbids attacking, and directs defensive preparations as the people assemble near Zarahemla and Bountiful.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records Gadianton robbers occupying deserted lands and facing famine as Nephites gather in one body with seven years’ provisions. In the nineteenth year Giddianhi attacks; the Nephites pray, fight, pursue to the wilderness border, and Giddianhi is slain. Under Zemnarihah the robbers lay siege, but suffer scarcity and raids; they retreat northward, are cut off, many surrender, and Zemnarihah is hanged. The people praise God for deliverance.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records the Nephites’ full belief in prophets’ words, their repentance, and the capture and judgment of robbers, freeing those who covenant to stop murdering. It notes 25 years passing with many events not recorded. Mormon identifies himself, his record sources and plates, and states promises of blessing and future gathering and restoration of the house of Jacob and seed of Joseph through Jesus Christ.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records the Nephites’ return to their lands after war, granting lands to repentant robbers, and a period of peace under Gidgiddoni and Lachoneus with rebuilt cities and roads. It covers rising pride, inequality, and the breakup of the church. Lachoneus’s son governs as prophets preach of Christ; judges secretly execute some. Complaints arise, and judges, lawyers, and high priests form a secret covenant to oppose justice, kill the governor, and establish a king.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records the murder of the chief judge, the collapse of Nephite government, and the people dividing into tribes with separate leaders and laws. A secret combination under Jacob retreats north to build a kingdom. Prophets are stoned and cast out. Nephi preaches repentance and faith in Jesus Christ, performs exorcisms, miracles, and raises his brother. Some convert; baptism by water is established and many are baptized.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records the passing of the 33rd year and the people’s expectation of Samuel’s prophesied three days of darkness amid doubts. In the 34th year a unprecedented storm brings tempests, thunder, lightning, earthquakes, and widespread destruction: Zarahemla burns, Moroni sinks into the sea, and Moronihah is buried under a mountain. After about three hours, thick darkness covers the land for three days, causing mourning and cries of repentance.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records a voice speaking to all the land, pronouncing woe and urging repentance after widespread destructions. It names cities destroyed by fire, sinking, burial, or flooding, including Zarahemla, Moroni, Moronihah, Gilgal, Onihah, Mocum, Jerusalem, Gadiandi, Gadiomnah, Jacob, Gimgimno, Jacobugath, Laman, Josh, Gad, and Kishkumen. Jesus Christ identifies himself, offers mercy and eternal life, fulfills the law of Moses, ends blood sacrifices, and commands offering a broken heart and contrite spirit.

This chapter contains 19 verses and records the people’s silence after the voice from heaven, then a renewed voice calls the house of Israel to repent, promising gathering or desolation. After three days the darkness and earthquakes cease and survivors turn from mourning to praise of Jesus Christ. It states prophecies are fulfilled, the more righteous are spared, cites Zenos, Zenock, and Jacob, and foreshadows Christ’s manifestation to Nephites and spared Lamanites.

This chapter contains 41 verses and records a multitude at the Bountiful temple hearing the Father’s voice introduce His Beloved Son, Jesus Christ, who descends and invites them to feel His wounds. The people worship, and Jesus gives Nephi and others authority to baptize, provides the baptismal wording, forbids disputations and contention, and declares His doctrine: repent, believe, be baptized, and become as a child.

This chapter contains 48 verses and records Jesus blessing those who heed the chosen twelve, believe, repent, and are baptized, promising baptism of fire and the Holy Ghost. He gives beatitudes, calls disciples salt and light, and states he fulfills the law. He commands reconciliation, warns against anger, lust, divorce without fornication, and swearing oaths, teaches nonretaliation, generosity, love of enemies, and urges perfection.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records Jesus’ instructions on giving alms, praying, and fasting in secret rather than for public praise. It gives a model prayer and commands forgiveness of others. It warns against storing earthly treasures, serving God and Mammon, and having an evil eye. Jesus charges the twelve to minister and teaches not to worry about food, drink, or clothing, but to seek God’s kingdom first.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records Jesus teaching the multitude to avoid judging others and to remove personal faults first; to not give holy things to dogs or pearls to swine; to ask, seek, and knock for blessings; and to treat others as one wishes to be treated. He teaches the strait gate and narrow way, warns of false prophets known by their fruits, and contrasts doing God’s will with mere claims, concluding with wise and foolish builders.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records Jesus explaining that the law of Moses is fulfilled in him and has an end, while prophecies and covenants continue to be fulfilled. He commands the people to keep his commandments and endure to the end for eternal life. He identifies the twelve as disciples and a light to a remnant of Joseph, in their promised land, and explains “other sheep” as separated Israelite groups, not Gentiles.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records Jesus saying he has other sheep elsewhere and will visit them by the Father’s command. He commands the Nephites to write his words to be preserved and manifested to the Gentiles, bringing scattered Israel to knowledge and a gathering. It blesses believing Gentiles, warns unbelieving Gentiles, and states the gospel will return to Israel. It affirms this land as Israel’s inheritance and quotes Isaiah about Zion’s restoration.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Jesus telling the multitude to go home, ponder his words, pray for understanding, and prepare for his return; he says he will go to the Father and to the lost tribes of Israel. Seeing their tears, he invites the sick and afflicted to be brought and heals them all. The people worship him; he brings and blesses the children, prays, weeps, and angels descend to minister to them.

This chapter contains 39 verses and records Jesus instituting the sacrament with bread and wine among the disciples and multitude, commanding it be done in remembrance of his body and blood, and promising his Spirit to those who always remember him. He commands watchfulness and continual prayer, family prayer, meeting often, and welcoming seekers. He instructs disciples to forbid unworthy partaking without casting people out, to minister and pray for them, warns against disputations, gives disciples power to give the Holy Ghost, and ascends into heaven.

This chapter contains 36 verses and records the people gathering again after Jesus ascends, as the twelve chosen disciples teach, organize the multitude, and lead prayer in Jesus’s name. Nephi is baptized and then baptizes the other disciples; the Holy Ghost falls on them with fire, and angels minister. Jesus appears, commands kneeling and prayer, and prays to the Father for the disciples and future believers, noting their great faith.

This chapter contains 46 verses and records Jesus ending vocal prayer, instructing continual prayer in the heart, and miraculously providing and administering bread and wine to disciples and the multitude. He teaches of his body and blood and speaks of fulfilling Isaiah and the Father’s covenants: gathering scattered Israel, establishing a New Jerusalem, Gentile blessings and judgment for impenitence, and Jerusalem’s future redemption and inheritance.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records Jesus giving a sign of the Father’s work to gather scattered Israel and reestablish Zion. He says the revealed words come to Gentiles, who are commanded to repent, believe, and be baptized or be cut off. A protected servant brings forth the message. The remnant of Jacob is among Gentiles; judgments remove warfare, idolatry, and wickedness. Repentant Gentiles join the covenant, help build New Jerusalem, and assist the gathering from all nations.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records the Lord’s promises to a barren and forsaken people to enlarge, break forth, and inherit the Gentiles. It commands them not to fear or be ashamed and identifies the Lord of Hosts as Maker and Redeemer. It states temporary forsaking followed by gathering, mercy, and an enduring covenant of peace. It describes Zion’s future establishment, children taught of the Lord, protection from enemies, and that no weapon prospers.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records Jesus commanding the people to search Isaiah and the prophets, heed his words, and write his teachings to later go to the Gentiles. He states that those who hearken, repent, and are baptized are saved. He has Nephi bring the records, notes Samuel the Lamanite’s prophecy about saints rising and appearing, and commands that omitted fulfillment be written. Jesus then commands the disciples to teach what he has expounded.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records Jesus commanding the people to write and hear Malachi’s words: the Lord sends a messenger to prepare the way and comes to his temple to refine and judge. It lists sins condemned, calls Israel to return, and accuses them of robbing God in tithes and offerings. It commands bringing tithes to the storehouse with promised blessings, records faithful people, a book of remembrance, and a future distinction between righteous and wicked.

This chapter contains 6 verses and covers the coming day of the Lord that burns the proud and wicked, while those who fear God receive healing and triumph. It records that the righteous tread down the wicked. It commands remembering the law of Moses given at Horeb. It foretells sending Elijah before the great and dreadful day, to turn fathers’ and children’s hearts.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records Jesus expounding all things to the multitude, including future events through the final judgment and resurrection. Mormon states only a small part of Jesus’s teachings is written; greater things are withheld or revealed based on faith, and the Lord forbids recording some sayings. Jesus teaches three days, appears often, breaks bread, heals, raises a man, and ascends. Children speak forbidden words. Disciples baptize; converts receive the Holy Ghost, live justly with all things common, and are called the church of Christ.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records Jesus appearing to his disciples during prayer and fasting, answering a dispute by directing the church be called in his name and built on his gospel. He defines his gospel, commands repentance, baptism, and enduring to the end, and warns of being hewn down. He commands them to write, teaches judgment by written records, instructs disciples to be like him, promises answers to prayer, foretells later generations’ decline, and teaches the strait gate.

This chapter contains 40 verses and records Jesus asking the Nephite disciples what they desire after his departure. Nine request to end their ministry and come to him at age seventy-two; three desire to remain and bring souls to Christ and are promised they will not taste death. They are transfigured, forbidden to reveal what they see, and continue ministering, baptizing, and giving the Holy Ghost. They escape prisons, pits, furnaces, and beasts unharmed; Mormon notes their future ministry among Gentiles, Jews, and Israel and explains their bodily change until judgment.

This chapter contains 9 verses and records that when these sayings come to the Gentiles it signals the Father’s covenant with Israel and their restoration is beginning. It states prophetic words will be fulfilled and the Lord remembers his covenant. It warns against spurning the Lord’s works, denying Christ, revelations, prophecy, gifts, tongues, healings, and miracles. It forbids mocking Jews or Israel’s remnant and affirms impending judgment.

This chapter contains 2 verses and records Mormon relaying Jesus Christ’s commanded message to the Gentiles: to turn from wickedness and specific sins including lying, whoredoms, secret abominations, idolatry, murder, priestcraft, envy, and strife; to come to Christ and be baptized in his name for remission of sins, receive the Holy Ghost, and be numbered with the house of Israel.

This chapter contains 49 verses and records the disciples of Jesus organizing the church, baptizing repentant converts, and a period of unity where Nephites and Lamanites have all things common, rebuild cities including Zarahemla, and experience miracles. It tracks record keepers (Nephi, Amos, Amos) as prosperity leads to pride, class divisions, and rival churches that persecute believers, including the three tarrying disciples. It describes renewed ethnic divisions, rise of Gadianton combinations, widespread wickedness, and Ammaron hiding the sacred records.

This chapter contains 19 verses and records Mormon beginning his record and recounting Ammaron’s charge to retrieve the plates at hill Shim in Antum. Mormon moves to Zarahemla; wars begin near Sidon between Nephites and Lamanites, followed by four years of peace. Wickedness spreads; disciples are taken away and miracles cease. Mormon is visited of the Lord but is forbidden to preach. Gadianton robbers, hidden treasures, sorceries, and witchcrafts increase.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records Mormon being appointed Nephite army leader at age 16 as wars resume with the Lamanites. Nephites retreat north, losing Angola and the lands of David and Joshua, amid widespread robbers and bloodshed. Mormon defeats Lamanite king Aaron, but Nephite sorrow is not true repentance. Mormon retrieves the Nephi plates near Jashon and continues his record. Nephites fortify Shem, win battles without the Lord’s strength, regain lands, then make a treaty dividing territory at the narrow passage.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records Mormon preparing the Nephites for war, calling them to repent, be baptized, and rebuild Christ’s church, and noting their refusal. The Lamanite king sends notice of renewed battle; the Nephites gather and fortify at Desolation and win battles in years 361–362. The Nephites boast and swear vengeance; Mormon resigns command. The Lord declares unrepentant Nephites will be cut off. Mormon addresses Gentiles, Israel, and remnants about judgment and the gospel witness.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records Nephite-Lamanite battles from years 363–375. Nephites are driven from and regain Desolation, gather at Teancum, and suffer heavy casualties and prisoners. Lamanites capture Desolation and Teancum, sacrifice captive women and children to idols, and later return with vast numbers, defeating Nephites at Desolation and Boaz. Mormon goes to hill Shim to retrieve Ammaron’s hidden records.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records Mormon resuming command of the Nephite armies, defensive battles at the city of Jordan, widespread Lamanite destruction of ungathered settlements, and a crushing defeat and flight in the 380th year. Mormon explains he writes an abridgment for the remnant of Jacob and the Gentiles, to come forth by commandment, persuade Jews that Jesus is the Christ, and address scattering and covenant remembrance. He calls Gentiles to repent.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records Mormon gathering the remaining Nephites at Cumorah by agreement with the Lamanite king, then hiding the sacred records in the hill and giving plates to Moroni. The Lamanites attack; the Nephites are largely slain, with Mormon wounded and only 24 survivors. Mormon lists fallen leaders with their ten thousand. He laments the destruction and references resurrection and judgment before Christ.

This chapter contains 10 verses and records Mormon addressing the spared remnant of the house of Israel. He states they are Israel and must repent to be saved, lay down weapons, and stop shedding blood unless God commands. He urges belief in Jesus Christ’s death and resurrection, teaching resurrection and judgment. He commands repentance and baptism, referencing additional records, and identifies them as Jacob’s remnant of the first covenant.

This chapter contains 41 verses and records Moroni finishing Mormon’s record after Cumorah, reporting the Nephites’ destruction, Mormon’s death, and Moroni alone hiding the plates. He notes ongoing Lamanite violence and ministry from surviving disciples of Jesus. Moroni explains the record’s purpose and limits, warns against condemning it, urges searching Isaiah, and prophesies the record coming forth amid denied miracles, wars, disasters, secret combinations, corrupt churches, pride, and neglect of the poor.

This chapter contains 37 verses and records Moroni warning unbelievers about Christ’s coming, judgment, and guilt before God, urging repentance and faith in Jesus Christ. It addresses denial of revelation and miracles, affirming God’s unchanging nature, creation, the Fall, redemption, resurrection, and final judgment. It cites signs following believers and commands preaching, baptism, and worthy sacrament. Moroni explains record imperfections, reformed Egyptian language, interpretation means, and prays for Israel’s covenant and restoration.

This chapter contains 43 verses and records Moroni’s abridgment from the plates of Ether, stating he omits creation-to-tower material and gives Ether’s Jaredite genealogy. It recounts Jared and his brother leaving the great tower after languages are confounded, the brother of Jared praying that their language and their friends’ language are not confounded, and the Lord commanding them to gather families, flocks, and seeds, travel north to a valley, and be led to a choice land where a great nation is promised.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Jared’s group traveling to the valley of Nimrod with flocks, fowls, fish, honey bees, and seeds. The Lord speaks to the brother of Jared in a cloud, directs them through wilderness and across waters, and declares decrees about a promised land. They camp at Moriancumer four years; the Lord chastens and forgives. They build tight barges; the Lord instructs air holes and asks how to provide light.

This chapter contains 28 verses and records the brother of Jared making sixteen clear stones on mount Shelem and asking the Lord to touch them to give light for eight vessels. The Lord touches the stones; the brother of Jared sees the Lord’s finger and then is shown the Lord, who identifies himself as Jesus Christ and speaks of creation and redemption. The brother of Jared is shown all inhabitants of the earth and commanded to write, seal, and hide these things and two stones for future revelation.

This chapter contains 19 verses and records that the brother of Jared’s visions are written, sealed, and withheld until after Christ’s ministry, then hidden again because of unbelief. Moroni seals the record and interpreters, to come forth to Gentiles upon repentance and faith. Jesus warns against contention and denial, describes his power, and promises Spirit manifestations to believers. Gentiles and Israel are commanded to repent, come to Christ, be baptized, and be faithful.

This chapter contains 6 verses and records Moroni stating he writes commanded words and seals up things that others are forbidden to touch for translation except by God’s wisdom. He says the plates may be shown to helpers, and to three witnesses by God’s power, establishing truth by their testimony. It notes Father, Son, and Holy Ghost bear record, repentance brings reception into God’s kingdom, and all stand before God at the last day.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records the Jaredite voyage in barges lit by shining stones, driven by a continual wind through tempests for 344 days to the promised land. The people land, worship, till the earth, multiply, and list Jared’s sons. As Jared and his brother age, the people request a king; Pagag and others refuse, and Orihah is anointed. Jared and his brother die; Orihah rules prosperously and teaches the people.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records Jaredite succession and conflicts: Orihah reigns and begets Kib; Corihor rebels, gathers an army in Nehor, and captures Kib at Moron. In captivity Kib begets Shule, who forges steel swords at hill Ephraim, defeats Corihor, restores Kib, and reigns. Noah rebels, captures Shule, but Shule’s sons kill Noah and restore Shule. The land divides; Shule defeats Cohor; Nimrod yields his kingdom. Prophets warn of idolatry; Shule protects them, enacts a law, and the people repent and prosper.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records Omer’s reign, Jared’s rebellion, and Omer’s captivity and restoration. Jared’s daughter proposes using Akish to assassinate Omer, and Akish forms a secret combination with oaths to gain power. Moroni warns that such combinations promote murder and plunder, cause national destruction, and commands Gentiles to repent and oppose them.

This chapter contains 35 verses and records Akish’s secret combination overthrowing Omer; Omer flees to Ablom, Jared is made king, then Jared and Akish’s rivals are murdered. Civil war between Akish and his sons nearly destroys the people, and Omer returns. Emer reigns prosperously, lists animals and riches, and Coriantum, Com, and Heth succeed. Heth kills Com, rejects prophets, and famine, drought, and serpents drive migration southward; the people repent and rain returns.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records Jaredite kings from Shez to Com, including rebuilding after famine, city-building, taxation oppression under Riplakish, rebellion and war, and Morianton’s rise to rule. It covers Kim’s captivity, Levi’s return to kingship, righteous reigns of Corom, Kish, and Lib, the destruction of poisonous serpents, settlement by the narrow neck, prosperity and industry, Hearthom’s loss of the kingdom, generations in captivity, Com’s wars to reunite the kingdom, and the rise of robbers and secret oaths.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records prophets warning King Com’s people to repent; the people reject them and seek to kill them, so they flee to Com. It recounts reigns and conflicts under Shiblom, Seth, Ahah, Ethem, Moron, and Coriantor, including wars, famine, pestilence, and executions of prophets. Secret combinations fuel rebellions, overthrows, and long captivities. Prophets also foretell utter destruction and another people possessing the land. Coriantor begets Ether.

This chapter contains 41 verses and records Ether prophesying to Coriantumr’s people to believe in God and repent. Moroni explains faith as hope for unseen things and cites miracles by faith (Alma and Amulek, Nephi and Lehi, Ammon, the three disciples, and the brother of Jared). Moroni speaks with the Lord about weakness in writing; the Lord teaches grace, humility, and making weak things strong through faith. Moroni defines charity, prays for the Gentiles, testifies he has seen Jesus, and exhorts all to seek Christ.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records Moroni’s summary of Ether’s rejected prophecies about a choice land, the New Jerusalem on this land, and the rebuilding of old Jerusalem for Israel. It describes Ether hiding in a rock as wars and secret combinations spread. The Lord commands Ether to warn Coriantumr to repent or face total destruction. Coriantumr refuses; Shared battles him, captures him, is later slain in the valley of Gilgal, and wounds Coriantumr.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records a curse on the land causing loss of property and distrust. After Shared dies, his brother Gilead fights Coriantumr, seizes Moron, and is murdered; Lib gains the kingdom. Coriantumr battles Lib, who is killed on the plains of Agosh; Shiz succeeds and devastates cities while pursuing Coriantumr. Massive casualties accumulate; Coriantumr fights near Corihor, Shurr, and hill Comnor, is wounded, and Shiz halts pursuit.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records Coriantumr’s sorrow and repentance after massive Jaredite casualties, his letters with Shiz proposing surrender, and continued warfare. The armies gather at the waters of Ripliancum, Ogath, and near hill Ramah, fighting for days until only a few remain. Shiz pursues Coriantumr; Coriantumr beheads Shiz and collapses. Ether witnesses, finishes his record, and hides it for Limhi’s people to find.

This chapter contains 4 verses and records Moroni’s situation after finishing the Jaredite abridgment. He remains alive but hides from the Lamanites to avoid being killed. He reports fierce Lamanite wars and that they execute Nephites who will not deny Christ. Moroni refuses to deny Christ, wanders for safety, and decides to write additional things for possible future benefit to the Lamanites.

This chapter contains 3 verses and records Christ’s words to the twelve disciples as he lays hands on them and calls them by name. He commands them to pray to the Father in his name and promises power to confer the Holy Ghost by laying on of hands in his name. These words occur at Christ’s first appearing; the multitude does not hear, but the disciples do, and recipients receive the Holy Ghost.

This chapter contains 4 verses and records how disciples called elders ordain priests and teachers. After praying to the Father in Christ’s name, they lay hands on the candidate and pronounce an ordination in Jesus Christ’s name to preach repentance and remission of sins through Jesus Christ, requiring endurance of faith to the end. Ordinations follow God’s gifts and callings and are done by the power of the Holy Ghost.

This chapter contains 3 verses and records the manner elders and priests administer the sacrament bread to the church according to Christ’s commandments, kneeling with the congregation and praying to the Father in Christ’s name to bless and sanctify the bread, for participants to remember Christ’s body, take upon them his name, always remember him, keep his commandments, and have his Spirit with them.

This chapter contains 2 verses and records the manner of administering the wine in the sacrament, including a prayer to God the Eternal Father to bless and sanctify the wine for those who drink, that they remember the blood of Jesus Christ, witness that they always remember him, and have his Spirit to be with them.

This chapter contains 9 verses and records requirements for baptism: repentance, broken heart, contrite spirit, and taking upon oneself the name of Christ with determination to serve. It describes members being numbered, names recorded, and being nourished by God’s word, prayer, and reliance on Christ. The church meets often to fast, pray, converse, and partake of bread and wine. It outlines discipline for iniquity, removal from records, forgiveness upon repentance, and Spirit-led meetings.

This chapter contains 48 verses and records Moroni quoting Mormon’s synagogue discourse on faith, hope, and charity. Mormon teaches judging good and evil by the light of Christ and that actions require real intent. He explains faith in Christ brings good gifts, miracles, angelic ministry, and repentance, and commands baptism. He defines hope through Christ’s atonement and resurrection and gives charity’s attributes, urging prayer to be filled with Christlike love.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records an epistle from Mormon to Moroni addressing disputes about baptizing little children. Mormon reports seeking the Lord and teaches that little children are alive in Christ, not accountable for sin, and need no repentance or baptism. He defines baptism as for accountable sinners unto remission of sins and warns against perverting this doctrine. He also mentions conflict with the Lamanites and Nephite pride, spiritual decline, and impending destruction.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records Mormon’s letter to Moroni about a lost battle with the Lamanites, the deaths of Archeantus, Luram, and Emron, and widespread Nephite wickedness and loss of love. He reports atrocities involving prisoners from the tower of Sherrizah and crimes in Moriantum, plus deprivation of widows by Zenephi’s army. Mormon urges diligent labor, warns of destruction unless repentance, notes desertions, and exhorts Moroni to be faithful in Christ.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records Moroni’s final exhortations as he seals the records, noting 420+ years since Christ’s coming sign. He urges readers to remember God’s mercy and to ask God in Christ’s name, with faith, for confirmation by the Holy Ghost. He lists spiritual gifts and warns against denying God’s power. He teaches faith, hope, and charity, calls readers to come to Christ, and closes with farewell and judgment language.
